plan.concept: Shannon's discrete entropy H = -Σ p_i log2 p_i as a measure of choice/uncertainty, computed over a small editable probability distribution.
learning_outcomes: Compute H in bits from a probability vector and read each term -p_i log2 p_i as that outcome's contribution.
Verify H=0 for certainty and H=log2 n for n equally likely outcomes.
See that equalizing probabilities raises H and that zero-probability outcomes contribute 0 (0·log0=0).
plan.visual_strategy: A pipeline shows raw weights -> normalized p_i -> per-outcome contributions -> total H; bars show p_i and contributions; a sweep over one probability shows the H curve with the current point marked.
plan.misconception: Entropy is not the number of outcomes; it is the average surprise, so 4 outcomes with p=(0.97,0.01,0.01,0.01) give far less than 2 bits.

title: Shannon Entropy: Measuring Choice and Uncertainty in Bits
idea: Given a set of possible events with known probabilities p_1,...,p_n, Shannon asks for a measure of how much 'choice' or uncertainty the selection involves. He requires continuity, monotonicity in n for equal probabilities, and consistency under decomposing a choice into successive choices; the unique such measure is H = -Σ p_i log p_i. With base-2 logarithms H is measured in bits.
why_it_matters: H is the fundamental limit on how much a source can be compressed and how much information a symbol carries. It also quantifies uncertainty in any probabilistic model, from communication to machine learning.

equations.caption: Theorem 2: the only H satisfying Shannon's three requirements; K sets the unit.
With K=1 and base-2 logs, H is in bits.
Property 3 (Fig. 6): a choice split into successive choices gives the weighted sum.

symbols.meaning: number of possible outcomes (events), a positive integer
probability of outcome i, with p_i ≥ 0 and Σ p_i = 1
raw nonnegative weight for outcome i; p_i = w_i / Σ w_j
positive constant fixing the unit; K=1 with base-2 logs gives bits
contribution of outcome i, c_i = -p_i log2 p_i, so H = Σ c_i

walkthrough: Choose n outcomes and give each a raw weight w_i ≥ 0 (the controls).
Normalize: p_i = w_i / Σ_j w_j, so the p_i are a valid probability distribution summing to 1.
For each outcome compute its surprise -log2 p_i and its contribution c_i = -p_i log2 p_i (with 0·log0 = 0).
Sum the contributions: H = Σ c_i, the entropy in bits.
Check the extremes: if one p_i = 1 then H = 0; if all p_i = 1/n then H = log2 n.

explorations.title: Certainty gives zero bits
explorations.change: Set w1 = 1 and all other weights to 0.
explorations.observe: p = (1,0,0,0), contributions = (0,0,0,0) and H = 0 bits, while log2 n = 2 bits.
explorations.why: If one outcome is certain there is no choice; Shannon's property 1 says H=0 iff all p_i but one are zero, and 0·log0 is taken as 0.

explorations.title: Four equally likely outcomes give two bits
explorations.observe: p = (0.25,0.25,0.25,0.25), each contribution = 0.5 bits, and H = 2.0 bits = log2 4.
explorations.why: Property 2: for fixed n, H is maximized and equals log n when all p_i = 1/n — the most uncertain situation.

misconception.title: Common misunderstanding
misconception.text: Entropy is not simply the number of outcomes. With n=4 but p=(0.97,0.01,0.01,0.01), H ≈ 0.24 bits, far below log2 4 = 2 bits, because the outcome is almost predictable. Only when the outcomes are equally likely does H reach log2 n.

checks.name: Four equally likely outcomes give 2 bits

from_paper: Theorem 2: the only H satisfying continuity, monotonicity in n for equal probabilities, and the decomposition property is H = -K Σ p_i log p_i (Section 6).
Property 1: H = 0 if and only if all the p_i but one are zero, this one having the value unity (Section 6).
Property 2: for a given n, H is a maximum and equal to log n when all the p_i are equal (Section 6).
With base-2 logarithms H represents bits per symbol (Section 7).
our_simplifications: We restrict n to 2–4 outcomes and use raw weights w_i that are normalized to p_i, so the learner can never enter an invalid distribution.
We use base-2 logarithms and K=1 throughout, so H is always in bits.
The sweep view varies only w1 while holding the other weights fixed, then renormalizes.
quotes: Can we ﬁnd a measure of how much “choice” is involved in the selection of the event or of how uncertain we are of the outcome?
